titre: “The End of History?” (1989): Fukuyama Wasn't Announcing the End of Events
accroche: The article that gave its name to an era posed a question in its title, and did not say that nothing more would ever happen.
contenu_vulgarise:
In summer 1989, the American magazine *The National Interest* published an article by Francis Fukuyama titled “The End of History?” The phrase quickly went around the world, only to be most often misunderstood: people thought the author was predicting the end of wars, crises, or the news.

## A Title Ending in a Question Mark

The article's title is a question, and it is the 1992 book, *The End of History and the Last Man*, that removes the question mark. The article defends a precise thesis: the end of the Cold War might mark, Fukuyama writes, “the end point of mankind's ideological evolution and the universalization of Western liberal democracy as the final form of human government.” The word “history” does not refer to the sequence of events here, but to history understood as a coherent evolutionary process, in Hegel's sense, whose reading Fukuyama takes from the philosopher Alexandre Kojève.

## What the Thesis Does Not Claim

It does not say that liberal democracy will triumph everywhere, or that conflicts will cease. It says that no rival ideology now offers a credible alternative to it, which is debatable and has been vigorously debated, but is not the same thing as predicting a world without events. Fukuyama himself clarified afterward that his thesis did not rule out events continuing, with democracy becoming, in his view, ever more widespread over the long term.

## Why the Nuance Matters

You can dispute the argument, and many have. But you dispute it better if you know what it says: a thesis about the end of ideological alternatives, not a prophecy of perpetual peace.

## An Article, Then a Book

The 1989 article must be distinguished from the 1992 book. The first is a hypothesis put forward as a question, which the magazine published in summer 1989: the text discusses Hegel and Kojève at length to say what an end point of the evolution of political ideas would be. The second develops the thesis at book length. Many readers criticize the book with a prophecy of peace in mind, whereas the article speaks of a process of ideas. Knowing who is being cited, Hegel reread by Kojève, helps explain why the word “history” does not have its everyday meaning here.

repere.texte: Fukuyama wrote in 1989 that the end of the Cold War might mark “the end point of mankind's ideological evolution and the universalization of Western liberal democracy”: the end point of humanity's ideological evolution, not the end of events.
repere.source: Francis Fukuyama, “The End of History?”, The National Interest, summer 1989

carte.punch: Fukuyama never announced the end of events, but the end of ideological alternatives.
carte.idee: “The End of History?” (1989) ends with a question mark and concerns humanity's ideological evolution, read in the manner of Hegel and Kojève. It predicts neither peace nor the end of the news.

quiz.question: What did Fukuyama mean by “end of history” in 1989?
choix: The end of all wars and all conflicts between nations
The end point of the evolution of ideologies, with no credible rival to liberal democracy
The gradual disappearance of nation-states in favor of world organizations
The definitive military victory of the United States over the Soviet Union
quiz.explication: In the 1989 article, which ends with a question mark, history is the process of the evolution of ideologies, not the sequence of events.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Which thinker, reread by Kojève, does Fukuyama draw on to give the word “history” its meaning?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The article discusses Hegel and Kojève's reading of him at length: history there is a coherent evolutionary process of ideas, not the sequence of events.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What distinguishes the 1992 book from the 1989 article?
choix: The book removes the question mark from the title and develops the thesis at book length
The book adds a question mark that the article did not have
The book appears in the magazine The National Interest, the article afterward
The book is published in 1979, ten years before the magazine article
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The 1989 article is a hypothesis posed as a question; the 1992 book removes the question mark and unfolds the thesis.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What did Fukuyama clarify afterward about events?
choix: That events would cease as soon as the Soviet Union collapsed
That his thesis did not rule out their continuing, with democracy spreading over the long term
That he was withdrawing his thesis, liberal democracy being in retreat
That only wars between great powers would disappear
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Fukuyama indicated that his thesis did not say that events stop: it concerns ideologies, with democracy ever more widespread over the long term.
